articles.title: Petries of Euboea - Epiphany and Christmas
articles.author: Τίτος Γιοχαλάς
articles.excerpt: Description of customs from Euboea for Epiphany, the blessing of fields and livestock, and the driving away of kallikantzaroi.

image.alt: Blessing of the waters at Epiphany in Euboea

content.value: On Epiphany day, we used to go to church to receive holy water, which we then sprinkled on our fields and livestock. We scattered the ash from the fireplace at the four corners of the house, all around the outside, to drive away the kallikantzaroi. We knew them from stories, but had never seen them with our own eyes. They said they had tails and feet that looked like those of donkeys. My mother used to say that once, in a big field nearby, the kallikantzaroi danced and sang at night. When darkness fell, people avoided going outside out of fear. The kallikantzaroi stayed among us from Christmas until Epiphany. Then the priest came, blessed the house with basil and holy water, and they left. The men sang carols, while the women did not participate.

articles.title: Velousia of Euboea - Kallikantzaroi - Christmas
articles.author: Τίτος Γιοχαλάς
articles.excerpt: Traditional belief from Velousia of Euboea about the kallikantzaroi and the Christmas protection customs.

image.alt: Illustration of kallikantzaroi according to folk traditions

content.value: The kallikantzaroi appear around Christmas and New Year’s. Until then, we kept the fire in the hearth burning day and night, so it wouldn’t go out and they’d come down the chimney into the house. The fire stayed alive until after Saint Basil’s Day. Then we cleaned out the ash, gathered it, and scattered it all around the house, to make the kallikantzaroi leave and not come back. We had never seen them, but they said they had tails. The old folks also said they had big ears and horns.

articles.title: Koskina of Euboea - Kallikantzaroi of Epiphany
articles.author: Τίτος Γιοχαλάς
articles.excerpt: Folk beliefs from Koskina of Euboea about the kallikantzaroi and Epiphany customs.

image.alt: Traditional image of kallikantzaroi from folk beliefs

content.value:
Who ever saw kallikantzaroi? On Epiphany day we got up very early. We cleaned the hearth and scattered the ash around the house to drive away the kallikantzaroi, because they would put out our fire with their urine and we couldn’t light it again.

We would light a new fire in the hearth to drive them out and force them to leave. In the morning, as we got up, we threw out the ash and said that the kallikantzaroi were burning with it.

The holy water came with the priest on Epiphany day, around eight in the morning. We sprinkled it on the vineyards so they would yield grapes and we’d have a good harvest. We also sprinkled it on the animals — the sheep, the cows, and the mares — so they would be healthy and fertile.

articles.title: Argyro of Euboea - Kallikantzaroi - Christmas
articles.author: Τίτος Γιοχαλάς
articles.excerpt: Folk beliefs from Argyro of Euboea about the kallikantzaroi and Christmas.

image.alt: Traditional image of kallikantzaroi from folk beliefs

content.value:
In my time I never got to see any kallikantzaroi. When we were small children, our parents would get up early in the morning — in those days there weren’t the things we have today — and leave an orange or some chestnuts under our pillow. They told us the kallikantzaroi had brought them, and we believed them. We believed it was them who left them for us.

We might even find a coin — back then only such coins existed, francs and small change.

articles.title: The Mill and the Kallikantzaroi
articles.author: Τίτος Γιοχαλάς
articles.excerpt: The story of a man who encountered kallikantzaroi while returning from the mill.

image.alt: Traditional image of kallikantzaroi around the mill

content.value: Once there was a man who went to the mill to grind his load. When he was done, it had already grown dark, and so he set off for home. As he walked, he thought he might encounter kallikantzaroi. To protect himself, he climbed up between the sacks on the animal’s back and covered himself with his coat so they wouldn’t see him and he wouldn’t get wet. The mule set off for home, and the kallikantzaroi looked all around — ahead, behind, left, right — but they couldn’t see any man.

They kept saying: ‘A sack from here, a sack from there, the trousers are in the middle.’

‘The master? He’s not behind!’ So they followed him along the road repeating the same phrase, puzzled that they couldn’t see the man. When he reached home and was unloading the mule, his wife came out, and as soon as the kallikantzaroi saw the dogs, they were frightened and ran away. Then they unloaded the rest of the cargo together, tied up the animals, and the master went to rest.

articles.title: Almyropotamos - Kallikantzaroi - Christmas
articles.author: Τίτος Γιοχαλάς
articles.excerpt: The tradition from the Almyropotamos area about the kallikantzaroi and the Christmas festivities.

image.alt: Traditional image of kallikantzaroi around the Christmas pig

content.value: When Christmas approached, we slaughtered the pig, fumigated it with incense, and hung it on a wooden pole from the ceiling to protect it from the kallikantzaroi, who were said to urinate on it. Our parents told us to be careful during the twelve days of the Twelve Days, because the kallikantzaroi were about. We weren’t supposed to go out at night or move far from the house. We gathered at home early because we were afraid they might catch us.

We were told the kallikantzaroi were black, with horns, a tail, and black feet, but no one knew exactly what they looked like. For protection, we collected the ash from the hearth for twelve days and kept it in a tin can. Then we spread it around the animals and in various places, to drive the kallikantzaroi away.

When Epiphany came, the priest passed through the houses with holy water, carrying a sprig of basil, and blessed the place, definitively driving away the kallikantzaroi. On New Year’s Day, we went to church and once the service ended, we exchanged wishes with the neighbours saying: ‘May we enter the new year well! Long life to us all! Happy New Year!’

articles.title: Beliefs about Kallikantzaroi - Raftaioi
articles.author: Τίτος Γιοχαλάς
articles.excerpt: The tradition from the Raftaioi area about the fire and the kallikantzaroi, used to make children obedient and attentive to their studies.

image.alt: The fire and the Yule log that kept the kallikantzaroi away

content.value: On the evenings of the Twelve Days, they would put a huge log in the hearth — so big it barely fit. The fire had to keep burning all night without going out until morning, to protect the house from the kallikantzaroi.

We would ask our grandfather why he put the big log in, and he would say that if the kallikantzaroi came, they would burn and leave. If there was no fire, they would come down the chimney and go in and out of the house.

Indeed, they said the kallikantzaroi punished children who were poor students — they would take their papers and stuff them down their backside! These were stories told as a scare tactic, to make children obey and study their lessons.

articles.title: Beliefs about Kallikantzaroi - Mesochoria
articles.author: Τίτος Γιοχαλάς
articles.excerpt: The tradition from the Mesochoria area about the kallikantzaroi and their connection to children's behaviour.

image.alt: The kallikantzaroi and the traditions associated with children

content.value: Our parents — our mother and father — told us that the kallikantzaroi would come and leave various things under our pillow: money, sweets, depending on whether we had been good children or not.
If we were studying, they would put pencils, pens, and things like that. But if we weren't being good children or weren't studying, then they wouldn't put anything under our pillow.

They warned us to be careful, because a kallikantzaros might come down the chimney. If we weren't well-behaved, the kallikantzaroi would come; but if we were well-behaved and studied, then Saint Basil would come and bring us our gifts.

articles.excerpt: The tradition of the Empousarioi of Kozani...

content.value: The Kozanite Charisios Megdanos (1800) confirms that this custom was more widespread, and that throughout the Twelve Days children carrying bells would go around to houses singing songs. Among their group there would be one or more people disguised with masks, bells, fox tails, and other similar things, with a strange and monstrous appearance, like that of the Empousas.
He adds that in his homeland, Kozani, these were called Empousarioi, slightly altering the name to fit the etymology from the word Empousa.

articles.title: Argyros of Samos - Kalampakis and the Kallikantzaroi
articles.excerpt: Account of a kallikantzaroi attack on Kalampakis after the death of his mother.

content.value: Kalampakis had accidentally killed his mother, and after this event he stopped going to church and participating in communal religious traditions.

One day between Christmas and Epiphany, while walking toward his hut at the location of Argyros, he noticed two men following him. He detoured from the main road and took a path toward his hut. There the two men rushed at him, stripped off his clothes, and smeared him with a foul-smelling substance.

His relatives started looking for him and found him in the hut, completely out of his mind. They took him to the Monastery of the Holy Trinity, where 40 days of prayer and fasting were needed before he recovered and could recount the kallikantzaroi attack.

content.value: A man passing at night through the port of Vathy saw ahead of him a hen followed by about 30 small white chicks. The man kicked the hen and it and the chicks suddenly vanished. At the same moment he kicked it, the man felt something was wrong with his leg.
The man in question died a few years later from a leg-related illness.

articles.title: The Kalispousides of Samos
articles.excerpt: Information about the kalispousides of Samos — spirits that punish blasphemers near water sources.

content.value: Many people reported encounters with kalispousides in Mytilinioi at the Agrias stream location. The kalispousides of Samos rush upon and devour those who blaspheme. They live near places with abundant water and near windmills.
The general belief is that they are malevolent spirits.
A more extensive analysis can be found in the books of Nikolaos Politis concerning the Kallikantzaroi.

articles.title: The Lykokatzaraioi of Arcadia
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk narrative about the mythical lykokatzaraioi and their eternal attempt to fell the tree that holds up the world.

content.value: The lykokatzaraioi come from under the Earth. All year long they hew with their axes to cut down the tree that holds the Earth.

They chop and chop, until they are almost there, with only the last branch left uncut, and they say: 'Come on, let's go — it will fall on its own.' They return after Epiphany, and find the tree whole and intact.
And they chop again, and they come again, and they do the same thing over and over.

articles.title: The Kalsangar of Tinos
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk explanation for the kalsangar and their connection to baptism errors in Tinos.

content.value: The kalsangar are not spirits — they are people who, when Saint Basil's Day approaches, are seized by a madness and leave their homes, wandering here and there.
Because in the old days priests didn't know their letters — they went from being ploughmen to becoming priests — and they made mistakes at baptism, and that's why people suffered.
They look just like ordinary people.

articles.title: The Pagana of Nafpaktos
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk narrative about the demonic pagana and protective practices against them.

content.value: The pagana enter the house through the chimney and through cracks, and they pour out the water and scatter the flour, but they are frightened of fire and chase after ash. For this reason, you must seal all the vessels at night, and when going to sleep throw heather or salt on the fire to make it crackle — the pagana flee from the noise they hear. Or throw a piece of hide to make it smell, and they won't come near.

Once I was sleeping in the fireside alcove, covered with the blanket right up to my head, and the fire had died down and it was dark. I suddenly woke up and saw in the glowing ember-light a pagano near the ash-box, scattering the ash; I grabbed it by the armpit, but it pulled away and took my hand with it, the cursed thing, and fled laughing up the chimney.

That is why the pagana-ash, which remains for as long as the pagana persist, is cursed. You must not use it for laundry because it shreds clothes, but you must throw away all you collect for as long as they are about, until they leave again and go back to the Underworld, to wrath and damnation.

And there, when the pagana descend, they begin to hew with their teeth and with axes the three pillars that support the world, to bring them down so that the world may be destroyed. They hew with great effort all year long, until — exhausted — they leave just one sliver uncut to catch their breath; but God gives them wrath and strips it away, and the pillars thicken and fill out again, and the pagana, out of stubbornness, then turn on each other and devour themselves.

articles.title: The Dance of the Lykokantaraioi - Kalamata
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk narrative about a woman's battle with the lykokantaraioi during the Twelve Days in Kalamata.

content.value: A woman from Dikalo, the village that is now deserted, was going to grind grain at the mill during the Twelve Days. She passed through a small hollow called Sola and saw lykokantaraioi dancing on a threshing floor.

She was very afraid they would eat her. There was no way to turn back, but she immediately thought of a trick to save herself. It was nearly dawn, and she knew the lykokantaraioi only had power at night, and after that they vanished.

If she could deceive them until daybreak, she could escape. She immediately pulled off her clothes and threw them on the ground, and naked she jumped into the middle and joined the dance like a lykokantaros.

At first the lykokantaraioi did not recognise her, but toward dawn they noticed something strange, because what they saw with their eyes seemed odd to them, and they danced wildly and sang and said with wonder: 'beard above, beard below, and trinkets in between!'

But just as they were about to look more carefully, day broke and they were forced to leave. And as they were leaving, they were saying: 'Let's go, let's go, for the old priest is coming with his holy-water sprinkler and has blessed us and covered us in sores!'

articles.title: The Karkantsaloi of Karditsa
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk narrative about the karkantsaloi and their destructive influence during the Twelve Days of Christmas.

content.value: The karkantsaloi have their dwelling in Hades, and they gnaw with their teeth the pillars that hold up the sky, so it won't fall and crush the earth. And gnawing and gnawing, they are almost cutting through the pillars.

They reduce them to the thickness of a woman's distaff, but the Christmas days overtake them, and they leave them and come up into the world. And by the time they return, they find them as they were from the beginning, untouched. That's how God wills it, because the world would be lost if the sky fell and crushed the earth.

And when Christmas approaches, they go into the world and wander through people's houses at night, from Christmas until Epiphany, and then they leave. Don't you know why priests go about on Epiphany Eve and sprinkle the houses? To drive out the karkantsalaioi — for no other reason.

Their leader is lame, and with his one leg he comes before the others who have two legs. In the old days the karkantsaloi appeared to people. Now we too have become karkantsaloi through our wickedness, and we can no longer see them.

And many people have suffered from them. So did the late Giannis Pipilagkous. But whatever happened to him, he brought it upon himself, because he thought it was foolish — what people do — burning wild pear branches or old sandals to keep them from approaching the house.

On Christmas night, when the church bell rang, he went to church and lit two candles, then came back home to roast the piglet he had prepared the evening before. When he got home, he made the fire and put the piglet on to roast.

While turning the spit, he saw a completely naked man entering through the flue — wearing only a wool cap pulled down over his head — with an iron spit on which a frog had been skewered. The figure went to the other side of the fire and turned his spit to roast the frog, the wrathful one.

While turning the spit, it said to Giannis: 'You drink and I drink.' Poor Giannis nearly lost his mind from fear; his voice was cut off and he couldn't breathe. Then the wrathful one bent down and urinated on the piglet.

And it took the spit in its hand and struck poor Giannis on the head, to kill him. Giannis jumped up and ran outside and told his neighbours, and went back with them to his house. But they didn't find the god-cursed thing.
They found only the piglet and threw it on the ground, lest some dog eat it and die, for it had been cursed by a karkantsal.

And many other people have suffered from them, but there is a remedy to ward them off and keep them from approaching people's houses. The remedy is wild pear branches and old sandals. For if one has any of these on the fire, that stench makes them unable to pass even through the neighbourhood.

articles.title: The Kallivrousides of Andros
articles.author: Θεοδ. Α. Βληζιώτης
articles.excerpt: Folklore study of the Kallivrousides (Kallikantzaroi) in Mesaria of Andros. These small demons appear at Christmas in underground storehouses, dance and urinate in containers with food. Inhabitants clean the storehouses and seal the containers with animal dung for protection.

content.value: The kallivrousides, or kallikantzaroi, are considered small demons who come out on Christmas Eve every year in the underground storehouses of villagers and dance. The inhabitants of the houses take care from the morning to have cleaned their storehouses thoroughly, because when they are very clean, it is believed the kallivrousides do not appear as often.

Every year when they appear, they urinate in the barrels and storage jars, usually over the figs. For this reason, all the containers are sealed using animal dung, creating a sticky mixture of water and manure.
The containers and barrels remain sealed until Lent, and there is a corresponding Christian prayer said at the time they are opened.

articles.title: The Kallikantzaroi of Spetses
articles.author: Rodd Rennell
articles.excerpt: Story from Spetses of a woman abducted by kallikantzaroi near a cave. She was found voiceless and recovered her speech only after a church exorcism.

image.alt: Traditional house in Spetses, setting of the kallikantzaroi story

content.value: A story was told to me in Spetses, which my informant had heard from his grandfather, about the adventures of a woman from the island with these strange beings.
She had gone with two other women to gather wood on the other side of the island, some distance from the town, near a cave by the sea, which is connected with various other superstitions.

But she suddenly disappeared, and all her companions' efforts to find her were in vain. Some days later, a boat passing the cape of the island saw the missing woman standing on the rocks. They came ashore and brought her back to town, but she had lost her voice and could give no explanation.

Only when she was taken to church and the necessary rites were performed for the exorcism of evil spirits did she recover her voice; and then she revealed that the Kallikantzaroi had seized her and had taken her voice so she could not reveal anything.

articles.title: The Kaoi of Rhodes
articles.author: Αναστασίος Βρόντης
articles.excerpt: Legend about the Kaoi (kallikantzaroi) of Rhodes. The priest Papagiannis from Monolithos caught a Kaos, healed him with lead and iron, and received a jar of honey in gratitude, known as 'The Kaos's Jar'.

content.value: In Rhodes the kallikantzaroi are called Kaoi.

Some years ago the priest of Monolithos, a man named Papagiannis, was coming one day from Kymmarasi (the village's harbour) and heard voices. He heard 'Kaou — Kaou.' He realised it was a Kaos calling out, and when he drew near he grabbed it by the hair before it could call out a third time.
He held it firmly by the hair and then the Kaos asked the priest:
— 'Tow or lead?'
— 'Lead,' answered the priest, and the Kaos curled up like a lamb. The priest took him to his house and burned its foot with a heated iron rod. From inside came dung-beetles (wild scarabs).
The Kaos then woke from its deep sleep and said:
— Where was I and where have I ended up?
The priest then asked where it was from, and the Kaos replied that it was from Tilos and lived inside an eggshell.
When the Kaos left and returned to Tilos, it sent the priest a gift — a jar full of honey. The jar is still in the house of Papagiannis and to this day (1939) is known as 'The Kaos's Jar.'

articles.title: The Old Man and the Lykokantзara at Megali Mantineia
articles.author: ΧΡ. Β. Φραγκούλης
articles.excerpt: Folk tale from Megali Mantineia, Messinia: an old man tricks the lykokantara in a cave with roasting meat, escapes, and with his wife's help finally drives them away.

content.value: Once upon a time there was an old man and an old woman. One morning the old man loaded his donkey with wheat and went to have it ground at the mill. The miller had a piglet and slaughtered it. 'Here, old man, take a piece of pork,' the miller said to him.

That evening when he set off to leave, he loaded his donkey, put the meat in his sack, and started out. On the road it grew dark while he was near a cave by the manor house. He climbed down from his donkey and went into the cave, where he lit a fire and began to roast the meat.

The lykokantara caught the scent and entered the cave. They pressed around the old man and asked for meat. 'Grandfather, give us a bite,' they said to him. He kept telling them to wait until it was cooked. 'Now, my son' — 'not yet' — he kept saying.
They began trying to snatch the coals. The old man kept giving the same answer until he grabbed a burning brand and struck them, burning them.
They farted and began running outside. Then the old man gathered his things and the meat, loaded them onto the donkey, and made off quickly himself.
To avoid being noticed, he covered himself completely with his cloak and from inside the cloak he held a stick to prod the donkey forward, while remaining hidden.

The lykokantara went back to the cave but didn't find him there and started running, catching up with the donkey. They looked here and there but couldn't see the old man and wondered where 'the old horn-head' had gone.
They ran back to the cave, looked, and didn't find him there either.
The old man had almost reached his house and shouted to his wife: 'Come out, old woman, with a firebrand!'
The old woman rushed out holding a shovel with hot coals, and seeing them approaching, she struck them with the shovel. They were burned and ran away.

That night, as the old man and old woman lay down to sleep, the lykokantara stuck their feet through the holes in the wall of the house, and the old man and the old woman, seeing them, were very frightened.

articles.title: The Old Woman at the Fountain and the Lykokatzara
articles.author: ΧΡ. Β. Φραγκούλης
articles.excerpt: Folk tale from Megali Mantineia: an old woman is caught by lykokantaroi at the fountain at night. They force her to dance naked, but she is saved when the priest's bell rings.

content.value: Once upon a time an old woman got up in the night, took her barrel, and set off toward the fountain to fill it with water before her grandchildren woke up. As soon as she arrived outside old Spanos's threshing floor, the lykokatzara grabbed her barrel.
Put down the barrel, they told her again. The poor old woman, having no choice, left it.
Then they told her to undress completely, and she was terrified but had no choice because they seized her and stripped her.

After stripping her, they forced her to dance with them. They all sang: 'beard above, beard below, and trinkets in between.' They told her to sing along with them. They began throwing her up in the air and from the air it seemed...

While they were dancing, the first cock was heard. The lykokatzara immediately stopped the dance. 'The bell,' said the youngest. 'Come on, it was just a cock — keep dancing,' said the others, and they continued.
After a while the bell rang again and the eldest said 'Now I heard it too,' and the others agreed.

'Let's go, let's go
For the old priest has come
With his holy water and his sprinkler
And has blessed us and defiled us'
They stopped the dance and ran away, releasing farts as they went. The poor old woman got dressed, put the barrel back on her shoulders, and went to the fountain to fill it with water.
When she returned home, her grandchildren were crying and asked why she was so late. Then the old woman told them what she had been through.

articles.title: The Kapsouria of Koukouli, Zagori
articles.author: Κώστας Π. Λαζαρίδης
articles.excerpt: Folklore study of the kapsouria (kallikantzaroi) in Koukouli of Zagori: the Twelve Days (24 December – 5 January), protective customs, regional names, and the activities of these demonic beings.

content.value: During the Twelve Days (24 December – 5 January), they do not wash clothes. When someone calls out at night from outside the house, those inside are not allowed to answer immediately without first making sure who called. There is the fear that the kapsouria will steal the voice of the person who spoke.

Anyone who absolutely must go outside at night should carry a small piece of incense. In the evening, before the family goes to sleep, a little incense is burned, because its smell keeps the kapsouria from coming near.
In the village the word 'kallikantzaroi' is not used. The names used are: kapsouria, katsina, doumhale, zizivoulides, exapedo, anavalтoi. The most common name is kapsouria.
The people believe these are demons (saitanaraioi) who come to earth during the Twelve Days with the sole purpose of causing harm to people.

They appear on earth on Christmas Eve and disappear on 5 January, as soon as the priest says the blessing 'In the Jordan...' During the Twelve Days they appear only at night, as soon as darkness falls, and remain until dawn when the cocks begin to crow. With the cock-crow they disappear, to reappear the following night — and so on.

In the village it is believed that the kapsouria have human form with various physical defects, mainly they are lame. That is why a lame person is said to be a 'zizivoules' or 'tzirtzivoules.' It is also said: 'The lame man and the devil are the same thing.'

It is also said that the kapsouria ride horses and donkeys. If someone suffers a small accident during this period, the women say: 'God keep us — that was the little zizivoules riding the donkey and not the big one riding the horse!'

When quarrels and fights break out in a house, people believe it is the invisible energy of the kapsouria. They say: 'There are the katsina, dancing now that the quarrelling has started in the house!'

The kapsouria wear ugly and tattered clothes on the nights they roam. That is why, when they see a person walking around dressed like that, they say: 'He walks in tatters like a katsoino.' And of someone who goes about at night: 'He walks at night like the kapsouria.'

The people also believe that the kapsouria love deep ravines, where they roam on the nights of the Twelve Days and beat drums and tambourines. Some women insist they have heard such sounds, and nothing will shake this belief.

They have a particular weakness for wandering near mills (water-mills). For this reason, millers do not sleep at the mill during this period and everyone avoids crossing bridges at night or spending the night near a mill.

articles.title: The Karkatзelia of Vrysika, Evros
articles.author: Ιωάννης Γουρίδης
articles.excerpt: Folk narrative about the karkatзelia (kallikantzaroi) who appear during the Twelve Days in Vrysika, and strategies for protection against them.

content.value: During the Twelve Days the karkatзelia (kallikantzaroi) also came out and troubled people. When the karkantzeli were about to come out from the underworld, they would say to each other: 'Let's go and roam about. The children have spread out.'

After roaming through the village and smelling meat somewhere, they would climb up onto the chimney. From there they would call out: 'You drink and I drink, come have a bite, it's even better.' Because no one answered them, they would leave.
Once, they say, an old man was coming home from the mill at midnight. From a distance he spotted the karkatзelia. To stop them from taking him, he wrapped himself in his cloak.

The karkatзelia climbed onto the cart and began to tease the old man to make him speak and steal his voice. They pinched him and said: 'This is a load, this is a load, what's this have got...' (obscenities).
But the old man did not speak, and so they were forced to leave.

articles.title: The Bride and the Karkatзelia
articles.author: Ιωάννης Γουρίδης
articles.excerpt: Story of a bride abducted by karkatзelia, and general rules for interacting with supernatural beings in Vrysika of Evros.

content.value: A bride was all dressed up and went outside at midnight. The karkatзelia grabbed her and began throwing her from one dung-heap to another and dancing.
They tried to make her speak. But she did not speak. The cocks crowed and the karkatзelia left and released the bride.
One must not speak to the zouzoula or karkantzelia, so they cannot take your voice.
One must not shoot at them, so as not to break one's weapon. With the cock-crowing they left.

articles.title: The Karkatзelia of Sitaria, Evros
articles.author: Ανάργυρος Εσκιτζόγλου
articles.excerpt: Protective practices against the karkatзelia (kallikantzaroi) during the Christmas period in Sitaria of Evros.

content.value: From Christmas Eve the kallikantzaroi also make their appearance — the “karkatzelia” — and in order to prevent them from entering the house, a branch of cedar is placed in front of it, the arditsi, as it is called; while at night people do not sleep near the fireplace, so that the “karkatzelia” shall not come in down the chimney, the so-called “paitzas”.
No work implement is carried into the house, so that the “karkatzelia” shall not follow it in.
Epiphany is awaited with particular joy, because the priest will come to bless the place, so that the “karkatzelia” shall depart.

articles.title: The Kallikantzaroi of Didymoteicho
articles.author: Α. Τσακίρη
articles.excerpt: Comprehensive description of beliefs, behaviours, and rituals regarding the kallikantzaroi in Didymoteicho of Evros.

content.value: During the Twelve Days people did not roast beans, did not roast corn, because the Karikatzeloi would come and tell them: 'We'll stick you in the carding combs.'

If girls went outside at night, they were caught and told: 'We want to make you a bride.' The girl would say: 'A bride needs many things. She needs a fine bridal dress. She needs shoes. She needs a veil. She needs a sack of gold coins.' The girl kept saying all these things slowly until the cocks crowed and the karkantzeiloi left and everything stayed with the bride.
They believed the kallikantzaroi were the joyful children of a king who danced, laughed, and sang all day. Some envied them, cursed them, and they became animals and kallikantzaroi.
From Christmas Day, the kallikantzaroi sit on the chimneys (batзadies) and leave when the Christmas holidays end.
When a child was born at Christmas, everyone believed it would become a kallikantzaros.
The kallikantzaroi roamed outside at night and went to the riverside. Whoever passed by, the kallikantzaroi would climb onto their shoulder and the person had to carry them to 7 wells.
The grandfathers said that at Christmas, the kallikantzaroi go underground and try to cut down the tree on which the earth rests, but they don't succeed.
Many women put baklava in the chimney and the kallikantzaroi came and ate it. Any woman who put baklava in the chimney stayed awake to try to see the kallikantzaroi.
One woman during the Twelve Days hung her clothes outside at night and the kallikantzaroi came and took them.

articles.title: The Karkantzaleoi of Pythio
articles.author: Α. Τσακίρη
articles.excerpt: Comprehensive description of the karkantzaleoi (kallikantzaroi) of Pythio, with protective methods and folk accounts.

content.value: Form and origin: They are like small people, black, with white hair and caps on their heads. They come from under the Earth. All year long they hew with their axes to cut down the tree that holds the Earth.
They come out at the birth of Christ and leave at Epiphany, when the blessing of the waters is sung. They enter houses through chimneys and urinate on all works in progress.

Methods of warding them off: They place a tall log in the chimney hearth and at the top of the log wedge a thorny branch, for the 'karkantzelia' to sit on so they won't think of coming down into the house.
Folk accounts: 'They come out as soon as night falls and leave at midnight when the cock crows. If they find you on the road at night, they torment you.'

They ask: 'What do you want?' I want a shirt, I want shoes, I want a headscarf, I want gold coins — all sorts of things. They change you and dress you as a bride if they manage it before the cocks crow; but if the cocks crow they leave you alone. If they manage to dress you before the cock crows, they throw you into the well and you are lost.

articles.title: The Katsikantarides of Chios
articles.author: Στυλιανός Βίος
articles.excerpt: A tradition from Kardamyla, Chios about the katsikantarides — the local Chian name for kallikantzaroi — who descend through the chimney during the Twelve Days and are tricked with a sieve.

image.alt: Tradition about katsikantarides in Kardamyla, Chios

content.value: The katsikantarides enter houses through the chimney (fouklaro) and leave again on the eve of Epiphany. They arrive on Christmas Eve and remain throughout the Twelve Days. To prevent them from entering the houses, people would place a sieve in the hearth, and the katsikantaris would begin to count its holes. But before he could finish counting them, the cock would crow and he would flee.
But if a fire is lit in the hearth, they do not come down, because they fear fire.
According to Irini Koukouna, from Kardamyla, aged 90.

articles.title: The Strigles and the Kalikazouria of Chios
articles.author: Στυλιανός Βίος
articles.excerpt: A tradition from Halki, Chios about the kalikazouria — those born on Christmas Day who become demons after death — and the strigles, girls with fire-shooting eyes who strangle and drain blood.

image.alt: Tradition about strigles and kalikazouria in Halki, Chios

content.value: Those who are born on Christmas Day, when they die, become kalikazouria and wander at night during the Twelve Days, tormenting people. Girls born on the same day become strigles, with eyes that shoot fire and great teeth.
These devour their own brothers. The midwives recognise them and strangle them immediately upon birth; but then they come out at night, and whoever they catch they strangle and drain of blood.
According to Irini Paliou, aged 60, from Halki.

articles.title: Tow or Lead - Kardamyla, Chios
articles.author: Στυλιανός Βίος
articles.excerpt: A tale from Kardamyla, Chios: a man catches a katsikantaris with a word game, keeps him occupied counting beans all night, and in the morning sends him off in an eggshell to Mytilini, from where the katsikantaris later sends a jug of oil.

image.alt: Tale of a katsikantaris in Kardamyla, Chios

content.value: A man was seized by a katsikantaris who asked him: "Tow or lead?" The man answered "Tow." And so the katsikantaris became light as tow, sat upon him, and the man carried him home.
There they bound him with a spartum rope, and then gave him a measure of wheat with beans — and the katsikantaris spent the whole day counting the beans.

But whenever he reached two, he never went to three — he would only say "one, two, one, two" — and so he counted until dawn. When dawn came, they gave him an eggshell; he climbed inside and made his way to Mytilini.
As he was leaving he said: "Fair winds, and I'm off to my place." From Mytilini, one year when the village produced not a drop of oil, the katsikantaris sent them a jar.
According to Anna I. Vios, aged 90, from Kardamyla.
